name: Prize crossword No 21,879
preamble: Fifteen of the across solutions and four of the down solutions (but not 41) are "Spoonerised". They have definition-type clues both of the original word or phrase and of how Spooner might have said it: and the Spoonerised form is to be entered in the diagram. For example, "Phantom missive from smugglers' foe (5,4)" leads to GHOST CARD (for COAST GUARD)

clue.text: Where Spooner studied (at Oxford) data about gardens and bridge?

blocks.note: Spooner was a fellow and later Warden of New College, Oxford; the preamble asks for the swapped form

explanation.surface: A fact about the great Oxford don's student days, plus something about gardens and a bridge.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the opening sounds of New College to get the entry. Kew is a London district famous for its botanical gardens and its Thames bridge.
explanation.definitionFit: Information concerning the Royal Botanic Gardens and the river crossing there is knowledge of that place, so Kew knowledge.

clue.text: A bit of spooning leads to a wedding, but no baby

definitions.text: A bit of spooning leads to a wedding

blocks.note: a pregnancy lost before birth produces no baby; swap its opening sounds as the preamble requires

explanation.surface: A courting couple's cuddle ends in marriage, though no child follows.
explanation.walkthrough: Spooning is old slang for kissing and cuddling, and also nods to Spooner himself. Swapping the first sounds of miscarriage gives the entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A kiss that leads on to a marriage is, in this invented sense, a kiss marriage, the phrase the swap produces.

clue.text: Anything for bric-a-brac

blocks.note: first meaning: any other unnamed thing, as tagged on to the end of a list
second meaning: a stand of open shelves for displaying ornaments, or the odds and ends themselves

explanation.walkthrough: Read as one phrase it sounds like a junk-shop offer; the two halves are separate senses of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means miscellaneous unnamed things, and is also an old furniture term for shelves holding ornaments and trinkets.

clue.text: Digital excrescences extracted from corpses?

blocks.note: growths on the digits of the foot; swap the opening sounds as the preamble requires

explanation.surface: A grisly mortuary scene of nails being removed from dead bodies.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'dead men tell no tales' says nothing can be drawn out of a corpse; toes are digits too, so toenails fit the first half.
explanation.definitionFit: The saying holds that dead people reveal no secrets, so what can be got out of corpses is no stories at all.

clue.text: Hero of comedy, the cock that cwowed?

indicators.note: this word is spelt the way a speaker who cannot roll the R would say it, with W standing in for R

blocks.note: a rooster is a cock, the male farmyard bird

explanation.surface: A comic hero is likened to a farmyard bird with a speech impediment.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the R of the bird for a W, as the misspelt 'cwowed' shows. Bertie Wooster is P. G. Wodehouse's comic hero, valet Jeeves's master.
explanation.definitionFit: Bertie Wooster is the bumbling central character of Wodehouse's comic novels, so he is a hero of comedy.

clue.text: River reaches sea - up the river the wrong way

indicators.note: letters arranged the wrong way are out of order and must be put right

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
R is the standard abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A river flows into the sea, but someone has gone up it the wrong way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'River reaches sea' reads as one statement, but only the first word is the definition and the rest is letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: The Euphrates is the great river of Mesopotamia, flowing through Turkey, Syria and Iraq to the Gulf.

clue.text: Officer, not private

blocks.note: first meaning: a senior army officer
second meaning: public, common to all rather than personal

explanation.walkthrough: 'Private' looks like the soldier's rank set against an officer, but here it means personal, so its opposite is public.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a top army rank and also an adjective for what is common or widespread rather than restricted.

clue.text: Wader forsook his status

blocks.note: a redshank is a wading bird with red legs; swap its opening sounds as the preamble requires

explanation.surface: A wading bird has given up its standing in the world.
explanation.walkthrough: Wader could be a boot or a person paddling, but here it is the shore bird.
explanation.definitionFit: To shed something is to cast it off, and rank is one's position or standing, so he abandoned his position.

clue.text: Sound horn at city on the way back

blocks.note: the road taken back to one's house; swap the opening sounds as the preamble requires

explanation.surface: A driver blasts the horn at a city while heading home.
explanation.walkthrough: To hoot is to sound a car horn, and Rome is the city.
explanation.definitionFit: Hooting is blowing a horn, and the Italian capital is the city, so the imperative phrase fits the instruction.

clue.text: Dog with job of silencer?

blocks.note: a silencer's task is to make the noise depart: noise, then go

explanation.surface: A dog is given work as a muffler.
explanation.walkthrough: Din is noise; a silencer's job is to make the din go, which run together spells the dog.
explanation.definitionFit: The dingo is the wild dog of Australia, so it is a type of canine.

clue.text: A yelp can work, no matter where

indicators.note: the letters can be worked into another arrangement, as clay is worked into a new shape

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written; it doubles as part of the signal phrase

explanation.surface: A dog's yelp is said to work wherever it is used.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' does double duty: its letters belong in the mix, and with 'work' it tells you to rearrange them.
explanation.definitionFit: Anyplace is American usage for anywhere, meaning whatever the location may be.

clue.text: Lamented about solvers being like eagles

indicators.note: to be about something is to surround it, so one word wraps round another

blocks.note: to keen is to wail in grief for the dead
the solvers are you, in the old form ye

explanation.surface: Someone mourns that crossword solvers are as sharp-sighted as birds of prey.
explanation.walkthrough: Keening is the Irish lament over a body. The setter addresses solvers as 'ye'.
explanation.definitionFit: Eagles are proverbial for sharp sight, so being like eagles means having very acute vision.

clue.text: Tadpoles will one day be causing cardiac arrest

blocks.note: something that stops the heart; swap the opening sounds as the preamble requires

explanation.surface: Tadpoles, one day, will give someone a heart attack.
explanation.walkthrough: Tadpoles grow into frogs, which hop, so one day they will begin hopping.
explanation.definitionFit: A tadpole becomes a frog and acquires legs, so its future is to begin leaping about.

clue.text: Exaggerated claims for obscenity in dance music

blocks.note: the hornpipe is a lively sailors' dance and its tune; swap the opening sounds as the preamble requires

explanation.surface: Someone complains of overblown claims about smut in club music.
explanation.walkthrough: Hype is overblown publicity, and porn is obscene material.
explanation.definitionFit: Hype is exaggerated promotion, and pornography is the obscene matter being promoted, giving overblown claims for smut.

clue.text: Tolerant worshipper needing doctor? No, not yet

blocks.note: MO is a Medical Officer
taken as written
what is not yet will happen later

explanation.surface: A broad-minded churchgoer asks whether a doctor is needed, and is told not yet.
explanation.walkthrough: The question and answer look like dialogue but are simply consecutive pieces of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: A monolater worships a single god without denying that other gods exist, hence tolerant of rival deities.

clue.text: See 8
See 31 across
The dog was on the catwalk, wrapped in cotton wool

definitions.text: The dog was on the catwalk

blocks.note: pampered and overprotected; swap the opening sounds as the preamble requires

explanation.surface: A pampered dog takes to the fashion runway.
explanation.walkthrough: A collie is a sheepdog; a model on the catwalk is modelling.
explanation.definitionFit: A collie is a breed of dog, and walking the catwalk is what a fashion model does, so the collie modelled.

clue.text: The ultimate comments could be the happiest

indicators.note: what letters could be is another possible arrangement of them

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A cheerful claim that last words might be the most joyful ones.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ultimate' is meant literally: the final words said about someone, carved on the tomb.
explanation.definitionFit: An epitaph is the inscription on a gravestone, the last remarks ever made about a person.

clue.text: Values or criticises the old way of tax-raising ...

blocks.note: first meaning: assesses or esteems
a further meaning: scolds, as in the old verb to rate someone
last meaning: the British local property tax replaced by the poll tax in 1990

explanation.surface: Someone assesses, or attacks, an outdated form of taxation.
explanation.walkthrough: Three meanings in a row. Rates were the property tax British councils levied until 1990; to rate someone is also old English for telling them off.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means assesses the worth of, and as a plural noun names the former British local property levy.

clue.text: ... which includes time left for use by noisy fans

indicators.note: to include is to hold within, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: the ellipsis carries the previous answer forward, so this word stands for it
T is the abbreviation for time
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: Continuing from 19, the old tax system now covers time set aside for rowdy supporters.
explanation.walkthrough: The dots tie 'which' to the previous answer, RATES. Wooden rattles were whirled by football crowds in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: A rattle was the noisemaker swung by football supporters, so rattles are things noisy fans use.

clue.text: God suffering from cavalier style

blocks.note: Pan is the Greek god of the wild
an ache is a pain one suffers

explanation.surface: A deity is in pain because of a swaggering manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suffering from' reads as one phrase, but 'from' is only the link.
explanation.definitionFit: Panache is flamboyant confidence, the dashing manner associated with the Cavaliers and their plumed hats.

clue.text: Shakespearean maid got up as vamp

indicators.note: in a down clue, getting up means rising from bottom to top, so the order flips

blocks.note: taken as written
a siren is a seductive woman, as a vamp is

explanation.surface: A Shakespearean servant girl dresses up as a seductress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Got up as' suggests a costume, but 'got up' is the reversal signal in a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Nerissa is Portia's waiting-woman in The Merchant of Venice, so she is a maid in Shakespeare.

clue.text: The perfect puzzler is a businessman

blocks.note: the setter of the puzzle refers to themselves as I
a businessman trades, so the setter is saying they trade, using the verb in the first person

explanation.surface: The ultimate crossword maker turns out to be a trader.
explanation.walkthrough: The puzzler is the setter, who would say 'I deal' if a businessman.
explanation.definitionFit: The ideal is the model of perfection, so 'the perfect' as a noun means the same as 'the ideal'.

clue.text: See 31 across
Gull in a twist of a tongue

indicators.note: something in a twist is tangled up and out of its normal order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, the same words also forming the signal

explanation.surface: A seagull gets its tongue twisted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a' does double duty: its letters join the mix, and 'in a twist' signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Lingual comes from Latin lingua, tongue, and describes anything relating to the tongue or to languages.

clue.text: I leave maiden's virtue corrupted: it shouldn't have happened

indicators.note: when something leaves, it departs and is no longer present
corrupted means spoilt and perverted from its proper form

blocks.note: the letter that departs
taken as written

explanation.surface: A seducer's confession of having ruined a girl's innocence, and his regret.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove one I from the phrase and rearrange the remaining twelve letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A misadventure is a mishap or unlucky accident, an event that ought not to have occurred.

clue.text: See 17
Comedy, maybe - have a drink first

blocks.note: a dram is a small measure of spirits, especially whisky
taken as written

explanation.surface: Before watching a comedy, have a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First' tells you the drink comes before the A, though it appears after it in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Comedy is one genre of stage play, so it is an example of drama; 'maybe' marks the example.

clue.text: Article that's extremely remote

blocks.note: A is the indefinite article
far means extremely, as in far better

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece described as very far-fetched.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' tempts one to take outer letters of a word, but it simply means far.
explanation.definitionFit: Afar means at a great distance, so something remote lies afar.

clue.text: Shed tears, my child, enough to drown people?

blocks.note: water deep enough to drown in; swap the opening sounds as the preamble requires

explanation.surface: A parent urges a daughter to cry floods of tears.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half is an instruction to a girl: cry, daughter.
explanation.definitionFit: To weep is to shed tears, and 'my child' addressed to a girl is daughter, giving the imperative phrase.

clue.text: Seemed pleased to have some good local colour outside

indicators.note: something outside goes round the other piece, enclosing it

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for good
a local is one's neighbourhood pub
red is a colour

explanation.surface: Someone looked happy because a place had good local colour all around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Local colour' reads as a single idea, but local is the British pub round the corner and colour is separate.
explanation.definitionFit: To grin is to smile broadly, so someone who grinned outwardly appeared pleased.

clue.text: Exciting and wicked puzzle completed in 1453?

blocks.note: 1453, the fall of Constantinople, is often taken as the end of the Middle Ages; swap the opening sounds as the preamble requires

explanation.surface: A thrilling, sinister whodunnit was finished in the fifteenth century.
explanation.walkthrough: The M of medieval and the H of history trade places; the first half reads as heady, evil and mystery in turn.
explanation.definitionFit: Heady means intoxicatingly exciting, evil means wicked, and a mystery is a puzzle, so the phrase matches word for word.

clue.text: Wine aroused craving in painter

indicators.note: to be aroused is to be raised up, which in a down clue turns the letters bottom to top

blocks.note: hock is German white wine, from the Rhine
a yen is a longing

explanation.surface: Drink stirred up desire in an artist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Aroused craving' sounds like passion, but 'aroused' just flips the letters upward. Hock is the British name for Rhine wine.
explanation.definitionFit: David Hockney is a famous English painter, known for his Californian swimming-pool pictures.

clue.text: I despise you! You disgust me! Make it with anchovy sauce!

definitions.text: I despise you! You disgust me!

blocks.note: a seafood dish under a pastry or potato crust, which a recipe might flavour this way; swap the opening sounds as the preamble requires

explanation.surface: An exasperated outburst at a cook, ending in a recipe instruction.
explanation.walkthrough: Pish and fie are old exclamations of scorn and disgust.
explanation.definitionFit: Pish expresses contempt and fie expresses disgust or shame, matching the two angry exclamations one after another.

clue.text: Singer with stout frame

blocks.note: the Welsh singer famous for Bond themes such as Goldfinger; swap the opening sounds as the preamble requires

explanation.surface: A vocalist with a sturdy build.
explanation.walkthrough: Shirley Bassey is a Welsh diva known for the Goldfinger theme; swapping her initial sounds gives the entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Burly means heavily built, a synonym of stout, and a chassis is a frame, as of a car or jokingly a body.

clue.text: Taking steel whip, repaired to bed

indicators.note: repaired means mended, put back together in working order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone took a metal whip and went off to bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Repaired to bed' reads as 'went to bed', but 'repaired' is the signal to rebuild the letters and 'to bed' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To bed someone is to have sex with them, an informal sense shared by the phrasal verb.

clue.text: An excursion gets aweigh

blocks.note: first meaning: read as two words, an outing
second meaning: nautical term for an anchor just lifted clear of the bottom

explanation.surface: A boat trip finally gets under way.
explanation.walkthrough: The first meaning splits as two words; the second is an old sailing term.
explanation.definitionFit: Atrip describes an anchor just broken out of the seabed, the same state as an anchor weighed.

clue.text: Young thing in the 'igh seas reportedly strikes the rocks

indicators.note: what is reported is heard rather than seen, so go by the spoken sound
being in means sitting inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: a cub is a young animal
the dropped H leaves 'eye seas', which spoken can be written as ICE plus ES

explanation.surface: A young creature on the open ocean runs aground.
explanation.walkthrough: A drink 'on the rocks' is served over ice, so the rocks are ice cubes. The dropped H mimics a Cockney accent.
explanation.definitionFit: In bar language a drink on the rocks is poured over ice, so the rocks are lumps of frozen water.

clue.text: Reduce about everything by a line to show latitude

indicators.note: to be about something is to surround it on all sides

blocks.note: to pare is to trim down
taken in its plain sense
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: Cutting things down along a line, in order to allow some leeway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Latitude' seems to mean freedom, but here it is the geographical sense; 'by' places the line beside the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A parallel is an imaginary circle round the Earth joining points of equal latitude, drawn on maps to mark it.

clue.text: Fish don't rise for a fool

blocks.note: the char is a fish of the trout family
to stay lying down is not to rise

explanation.surface: An angler's complaint that the fish won't bite for an idiot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rise' is what fish do to take a fly, so the surface is angling; here not rising means staying down. A charlie is British slang for a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a charlie is a silly person, as in 'a right charlie'.

clue.text: Acquires information without backing and money in the bank?

indicators.note: backing means moving backwards, so both pieces read from end to start
without in its old sense means outside, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: gen is British slang for information
to acquire is to get

explanation.surface: Someone gathers facts without support and has savings tucked away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without backing' looks like 'unsupported', but it means outside and reversed. Gen is British slang for the facts.
explanation.definitionFit: A nest egg is a sum saved for the future, and the question mark admits the bank is only one place to keep it.

clue.text: Language was difficult, said Denis (with his eyebrows?)

indicators.note: difficult letters are awkward and unruly, so they must be reordered
said points to the way a name is spoken rather than spelt

blocks.note: taken as written
Denis Healey, the Labour Chancellor famous for his bushy eyebrows

explanation.surface: Someone reports that Denis found a foreign tongue hard going, raising his eyebrows.
explanation.walkthrough: Denis Healey was a British Chancellor in the 1970s whose enormous eyebrows were cartoonists' favourite; his surname is pronounced like the end of the language.
explanation.definitionFit: Swahili is the Bantu tongue widely spoken across East Africa, in Kenya and Tanzania.

clue.text: City getting radiant heat from Spooner?

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words

blocks.note: the warmth radiated by a gas fire

explanation.surface: A city warmed by the Reverend Spooner's glow.
explanation.walkthrough: Unlike the others, this one names Spooner in the clue, and the swapped form is a real word.
explanation.definitionFit: Glasgow is Scotland's largest city, on the River Clyde.

clue.text: I'm agreeably surprised about record of leading character

indicators.note: to be about something is to surround it

blocks.note: aha is the cry of pleased discovery
an LP is a long-playing record

explanation.surface: A happy reaction to the record of a star actor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leading character' suggests an actor in the lead role, but it means the first letter of the alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Alpha is the first letter of the Greek alphabet, so it is the character that comes first.

clue.text: A place of work for the wrong sort of graduate around Birmingham

indicators.note: the wrong sort here means the wrong way round, written back to front

blocks.note: taken as written
a lab, or laboratory, is a workplace
MA is the graduate's degree, written AM in America; the extra A is not separately clued in a strict reading

explanation.surface: A workplace intended for the wrong kind of university leaver, near a British city.
explanation.walkthrough: Birmingham looks like the English city, but there is a Birmingham in the American state, which surrounds it.
explanation.definitionFit: Birmingham is the largest city in the US state of Alabama, which therefore lies all around it.

clue.text: Bear expressed contempt for pluralist

blocks.note: Winnie-the-Pooh, A. A. Milne's bear
bah is a scornful exclamation

explanation.surface: A bear sneered at someone holding many posts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bear' looks like a verb meaning tolerate, but it is Milne's famous teddy.
explanation.definitionFit: Pooh-Bah, from Gilbert and Sullivan's Mikado, holds a host of offices at once, as a pluralist does.

clue.text: "Yellow Bird" next century

blocks.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
the raven is a large black bird; it comes next after the hundred

explanation.surface: The title of a song, followed by a mention of the next hundred years.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make 'Yellow Bird' look like one title, but yellow is the definition and the bird is separate.
explanation.definitionFit: Yellow is slang for cowardly, and craven means contemptibly lacking in courage.

clue.text: Code - and this isn't English

blocks.note: et is Latin for and
hic is Latin for this, so the word is not given in English

explanation.surface: A cipher is offered, with the warning that it is not in English.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Isn't English' is the cue to translate the two short words into Latin.
explanation.definitionFit: An ethic is a set of moral principles governing conduct, a code to live by.

clue.text: Bird that says words such as "unimportant"

indicators.note: saying something is speaking it, so the sound matters rather than the spelling

blocks.note: minor is a synonym for unimportant

explanation.surface: A talking bird that utters dismissive words.
explanation.walkthrough: Mynas are famous mimics that talk, which makes 'says' natural in the surface. In non-rhotic British speech minor and myna sound alike.
explanation.definitionFit: The myna is a starling from Asia, kept as a cage bird for its skill at imitating speech.

clue.text: Comedy, maybe, one extended to humour?

blocks.note: a comedy is an example of a stage play
a means one
long means extended in length

explanation.surface: A long-running comedy offers something to laugh at.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Humour' looks like a noun about comedy, but it is the verb meaning to indulge.
explanation.definitionFit: To humour someone is to go along with their wishes, which is to cooperate without real agreement.

clue.text: Lactation takes minutes

indicators.note: to take is to draw out a part, so the letters are lifted from inside the word

blocks.note: the letters sit inside, after the first L

explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes minutes' sounds like time spent nursing, but minutes are records of a meeting.
explanation.definitionFit: Acta is the Latin term for recorded proceedings or official records, the same as minutes of a meeting.

clue.text: Restrain the daring dogsbody

blocks.note: to restrain is to keep in check; swap the opening sounds as the preamble requires

explanation.surface: An order to rein in an overbold drudge.
explanation.walkthrough: A hack is someone doing dull work for hire, a drudge, and dogsbody is British for the person given menial jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: Bold means daring, and a hack is a drudge hired for routine work, the same as a dogsbody.

clue.text: Equestrienne's cover, like Peter from Mr McGregor?

blocks.note: a horsewoman's long skirted outfit; swap the opening sounds as the preamble requires

explanation.surface: A horsewoman's outfit is likened to a storybook animal on the run.
explanation.walkthrough: In Beatrix Potter's Peter Rabbit, Peter hides from the gardener Mr McGregor, who would put him in a pie.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter Rabbit spends his tale hiding from the farmer in his garden, so he is a rabbit in hiding.

clue.text: The only nail to catch something for the salad

definitions.text: The only nail to catch something

blocks.note: shredded cabbage salad in mayonnaise; swap the opening sounds as the preamble requires

explanation.surface: A single fingernail is used to pick up a bit of the salad.
explanation.walkthrough: Sole means only, and a claw is a nail that catches and grips.
explanation.definitionFit: Sole means single or only, and a claw is a hooked nail used for seizing prey.

clue.text: The right sort of day for a battle given to a 44?

definitions.text: The right sort of day for a battle

blocks.note: a white feather was handed to men thought cowardly, which is 44's meaning; swap the opening sounds as the preamble requires

explanation.surface: A good day for combat is handed to a coward.
explanation.walkthrough: In wartime Britain, white feathers were given to men out of uniform to brand them cowards; 44 is CRAVEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Weather suitable for a fight is fight weather, the conditions right for joining battle.
